analysis.one_liner: Banned ATM owners from charging fees when consumers use another bank's cash machine.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died in the House Banking Committee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: When you use an ATM run by a bank other than your own, the machine's owner adds a fee on top of whatever your bank charges. This bill would amend the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to prohibit the company or bank operating the ATM from charging the consumer any fee for that transaction. It was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses an out-of-network ATM, especially people who cannot easily get to their own bank's machines and lower-income consumers who can least afford a few dollars lost to a fee on a cash withdrawal.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the operator of an ATM from imposing any fee on the consumer when the consumer's transaction runs over a national or regional network to a bank other than the machine owner's [S2][S3].
Amends the existing Electronic Fund Transfer Act, the federal law that already governs consumer protections for debit and ATM transactions, so the ban would be federally enforceable [S2][S3].
Targets only the surcharge added by the machine owner, not the fee a consumer's own bank charges, leaving that part of pricing untouched [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and companies that own ATMs would lose the surcharge revenue they collect every time a non-customer uses their machines. That includes banks, plus the independent companies that place ATMs in convenience stores, bars, and other locations.

drawbacks.text: Out-of-network transactions cost the machine owner real money in network switching fees and cash handling, so an outright ban could lead operators to remove machines from low-traffic locations like small stores and rural areas, or to restrict out-of-network use rather than eat the cost.
The bill addresses only one slice of ATM pricing — the owner's surcharge — so consumers could still face fees from their own banks, and pricing pressure would shift to other channels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is direct and easy to see: no fee at the machine when you withdraw cash away from your own bank. The honest objection is that if operators cannot charge for serving non-customers, some may pull machines out of marginal locations or limit access, and the ban leaves bank-side fees alone. A narrower fix — capping or disclosing the surcharge — was the more common approach in later years, but the bill as written was a clean prohibition in consumers' favor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee, which passed it down to a subcommittee in late February 1997, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on February 13, 1997 [S5][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services the same day [S5].
On February 28, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit [S5].
No markup, floor vote, or further action appears in the record; the 105th Congress ended January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and ATM operators, who kept collecting surcharges from non-customer users. In the years that followed, such fees became a routine, widespread charge on cash withdrawals nationwide.

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Cosponsors of H.R. 795 (23 House Democrats, 1 House Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; 23 Democrats and 1 Republican.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, passed it to a subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the only partisan signal is sponsorship: 23 of the 24 cosponsors were Democrats, with 1 Republican, under an independent lead sponsor [S4].

industries.industry: Banks and ATM operators (including independent ATM deployers)
industries.note: The bill would eliminate the surcharge they collect whenever a non-customer withdraws cash from their machines — a per-transaction fee paid directly by consumers. The bill died in committee, so this revenue stream was untouched, and surcharges went on to become a standard nationwide fee.
